title: Hong Kong Regulator Official Floats AI Agent to Flag Crypto Crime
excerpt: Raymond Chan, executive director for enforcement and anti-money laundering at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), floated a possible AI agent that could help banks detect suspicious crypto activity by linking blockchain transfers with customers’ offchain transactions. Discover more. Crypto market analysis. Blockchain news subscription. Bitcoin price tracker. Chan presented the specific on-chain agent as a thought exercise at a regulatory technology workshop Tuesday, Nov. 17. He gave no deployment timeline and did not say whether banks would be required to use such a tool. The concept would combine blockchain analytics, customer due-diligence information, scam intelligence and suspicious-wallet monitoring with rapid fund freezes. It could help banks flag fast, repeated exchanges between crypto and fiat, which can obscure the movement of money. Chan identified linking wallet activity to real-world identities quickly enough to stop funds from moving as a key challenge. Chan also said the HKMA is exploring agentic AI more broadly, referring to software that can carry out multistep tasks. On stablecoins, Chan described the HKMA’s initial approach as cautious, with investor protection and financial-crime controls as priorities. He said the authority is beginning to put its surveillance framework into operation and is exploring and piloting decentralized identity tools that can link a wallet to a verified person. Crypto flows to illicit addresses exceeded $150 billion in 2025, with stablecoins accounting for 84% of the total. He also pointed to Hong Kong’s Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce, a public-private channel connecting police, customs authorities, financial regulators, licensed virtual-asset service providers and stablecoin issuers. title: Arva AI Raises $20 Million To Automate Critical Banking Operations
excerpt: . Arva AI Raises $20 Million To Automate Critical Banking Operations. Arva AI has raised $20 million in Series A funding to expand artificial intelligence models and agents designed for regulated banking and financial technology operations. Arthur Ventures led the round, with continued participation from Y Combinator and Gradient Ventures. The company plans to prioritize investment in Arva Research, its internal model-development organization, while expanding its technology across banking back-office functions ranging from financial crime compliance to lending. The financing follows several large deployments, including implementations at a top-10 U. S. bank, an S&P 500 payments company, and Wise. Building Models For Explainable Financial Decisions. Banks make large numbers of decisions involving customer eligibility, financial crime risks, lending, transaction monitoring, and regulatory compliance. Many of these decisions still require manual review because financial institutions must be able to explain their conclusions to auditors and regulators. General-purpose AI models may produce inconsistent or unsupported answers unless people verify the results. Arva is developing proprietary models for decision stages where accuracy, evidence, and auditability are particularly important. The company’s first research model, Arva Intel, investigates businesses and individuals using online information. In Arva’s internal testing, the model produced accuracy results 13% better than leading general-purpose alternatives. Because this result comes from company testing, its broader performance will depend on the evaluation methodology, datasets, use cases, and models used for comparison. Arva Intel operates alongside AgentCore, the company’s continual-learning infrastructure. AgentCore adapts the system to an individual bank’s policies, historical decisions, and operating processes. The combination is intended to give banks AI agents that can perform research and operational tasks while producing results that institutions can review and explain. Funding Follows Arva Research Launch. Arva launched Arva Research in September 2026. The new funding will support continued development of specialized models for banking operations. The company’s strategy reflects a belief that financial institutions will require domain-specific systems rather than relying solely on general-purpose models. A banking agent must understand regulatory expectations, follow institutional policies, and maintain a record of how it reached a conclusion. Boston Consulting Group has estimated that AI agents could reduce banking costs by between 30% and 40% by 2030. Achieving those savings would require institutions to move beyond pilots and allow AI systems to complete consequential work reliably. Arva was founded in 2024 by CEO Rhim Shah and Chief Technology Officer Oliver Wales. Shah previously led financial crime products at Revolut Business, while Wales was formerly chief product engineer at Seal. Their backgrounds combine regulated financial operations with AI product engineering. Arva is initially focused on financial crime compliance and lending, but it intends to extend its models and agents across additional back-office processes. KEY QUOTES:. title: Plaid Launches Agent Detection Tool to Help Banks Identify AI-Driven Financial Activity
excerpt: Financial technology company Plaid has introduced Agent Detection, a new capability designed to help banks, fintech businesses and other financial institutions distinguish between interactions initiated by people and those performed by artificial intelligence agents. Announced on November 16, the product addresses a growing challenge as AI assistants begin navigating websites, accessing accounts and carrying out tasks on behalf of consumers. The company said the tool is designed to identify whether an interaction is human-driven or agent-driven and, where possible, determine which AI provider is associated with the activity. Identifying Automated Financial Interactions. AI agents can navigate websites in ways that resemble ordinary human browsing. This can make it difficult for traditional fraud-prevention systems to determine whether a login, account-linking request or payment interaction comes from a customer or an automated assistant. Plaid’s Agent Detection analyses thousands of signals across devices, user behaviour, automation patterns and network activity. Financial institutions can use the information to decide how to handle interactions initiated by agents, including whether additional verification or restrictions are needed. For example, a consumer may ask an AI assistant to pay an upcoming bill. A bank using the detection capability could recognise that an agent is performing the interaction and apply controls appropriate to that activity. Designed for Financial Services Workflows. The tool can be integrated through a lightweight software development kit across digital experiences such as login, account registration and money movement. Plaid said existing customers may also be able to access the capability through their current integrations with limited additional setup. The company reported that, in side-by-side testing on live traffic, its system identified 2. 3 times more agent sessions than competitors without an increase in false positives. This is a company-reported result and has not been independently established in the announcement. A New Layer of Trust for Agentic Finance. The launch reflects a broader shift in financial services as AI agents move from retrieving information to taking actions. Banks will need to distinguish legitimate customer-authorised activity from suspicious automation while maintaining clear rules around permissions and consumer control. Plaid said Agent Detection is available to businesses today. Its longer-term significance will depend on adoption by financial institutions and how effectively the technology supports secure, transparent agent-led transactions.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will further explore artificial intelligence (AI) agents and tokenisation, setting out plans for a new agent verification protocol, a new sandbox, and updated tokenisation guides. Whilst adoption of AI agents are still in the early stages, it has the potential to scale rapidly as the industry realizes that it can cut costs and ramp up speed of search and comparison, optimisation and decisions, negotiations and execution, said Chia Der Jiun , managing director of MAS, said in his keynote speech for Day 2 of the Singapore Fintech Festival (SFF) on 19 November. Join Singapore Business Review community. MAS said that it will work to develop a common protocol to verify agents’ representation and mandate, as well as a sandbox to explore AI agents and programmable money, Chia said. “The two initiatives I've highlighted, common protocols for agent transactions and the sandbox for agentic money, will be important building blocks for the future of agentic transactions,” Chia said. The common Know-Your-Agent protocol will require customers and financial institutions to exchange information about the agent’s identity, representation, authority, mandate it operates under, and provenance. MAS believes that this will give financial institutions the information needed to determine the terms and the scope of permission that the agents hold, Chia said. MAS is also setting up a sandbox with the Future of Finance Institute, bringing together AI agents and programmable money for corporate treasury management and payments services, he said. excerpt: New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities. The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services. Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing. Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector. The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI. By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions about adopting AI responsibly. Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'AI is creating significant opportunities across financial services, and we’re committed to helping firms understand how the technology is being used. 'The AI Spotlight Observatory provides an open and accessible resource that brings together real-world examples of AI adoption, helping firms, innovators and researchers learn from developments across the sector and identify new opportunities for innovation and growth. '. Notes to editors. The FCA’s AI Spotlight Observatory is the first resource of its kind for a regulator globally. It builds on the FCA’s AI Spotlight Digital Showcase, a repository of practical AI solutions across specific themes, by adding new features and capabilities, such as a common taxonomy for comparison, a distinction between use cases and implementations, and the ability to identify emerging patterns across the market. The platform is open and accessible to all users. Registration is required to access more detailed insights, such as target client information, and to request demonstrations directly from innovators featured on the platform. The Observatory will continue to evolve through the addition of new use cases. Firms can apply to be showcased on the platform. CFTE has supported the development of the Observatory across three main areas: creating the taxonomy, building the repository, and socialising the Observatory with the market. The Observatory forms part of CFTE’s wider collaboration with the FCA on AI capability, industry engagement and market intelligence. Alongside initiatives such as the Agentic Academy, CFTE supports the FCA in helping the financial-services sector better understand, structure and respond to the opportunities and challenges created by AI. NayaOne has been responsible for the design and development of the Observatory platform, including the user interface, navigation, search and filtering capabilities. The platform builds on the FCA’s wider work on AI, including its. AI Discussion Paper , AI Sprint , and AI Lab , which includes AI Live Testing and its groundbreaking Supercharged Sandbox supported by NVIDIA, NayaOne and Anthropic. Last month, the FCA published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services.

title: Hyundai Card and JPMorgan Test AI Agents’ Ability to Make Payments
excerpt: Hyundai Card and JPMorgan Test AI Agents’ Ability to Make Payments. By PYMNTS | November 18, 2026. |. Hyundai’s credit card arm says it has seen success from its blockchain payments partnership with Kinexys by J. P. Morgan. This effort has shown the potential for artificial intelligence (AI) agents to “autonomously and securely execute financial transactions,” Hyundai Card said in a news release provided to PYMNTS Wednesday (Nov. 18). The proof of concept (PoC) completed by the two companies was designed to “validate the feasibility of automating financial operations, including cash management, foreign exchange (FX) and fund transfers, through communication between AI agents ,” the release added. Hyundai said the PoC centered around simulated transactions between hypothetical overseas subsidiaries using AI agents to handle and transfer funds. Hyundai Card designed the transaction scenario and created the authorization and control framework for the AI agents. Using this framework, Kinexys developed the AI agents for both companies and implemented identity verification, authorization, control and validation mechanisms to secure transactions. “The PoC represents a first-of-its-kind demonstration of how AI agents can securely exchange information and execute financial transactions within a controlled environment,” the release said. “While conventional AI-powered financial automation has primarily focused on analyzing cash positions or executing transactions based on predefined rules, this PoC explored a more advanced model in which AI agents from different institutions communicate, make independent decisions and carry out financial transactions autonomously. ”. In other agentic AI news, PYMNTS wrote recently about a scenario in which a portal might reject an agentic payment. The report described a restaurant paying its food distributor, packaging supplier and equipment service provider. “An agent could submit all three approved payments if it has access to the suppliers’ systems and each payment meets the applicable rules,” the report said. “If the packaging supplier’s portal rejects the card, the bookkeeper may need to arrange another way to pay. If the equipment company’s portal shows a higher balance than the approved invoice, someone has to check whether the supplier revised the bill or whether the portal includes another charge. ”. A supplier may also grant a discount in exchange for getting paid earlier. Tungsten Automation CEO Peter Hantman told PYMNTS that the gap between invoice approval and payment is an opportunity to examine such offers. Research by PYMNTS Intelligence shows that fewer bills are being paid ahead of schedule among larger businesses, with the share of payables paid early dropping from 37% to 17% between editions of the Working Capital Index. “For a buyer paying on the due date, a portal rejection leaves less time to correct the problem,” the report said. “If two of the restaurant’s three payments go through, the bookkeeper needs to know which supplier is still waiting and whether the third payment failed because of the card, the invoice or the portal. ”. title: OCC Brings Agentic AI Into Bank Examinations
excerpt: OCC Brings Agentic AI Into Bank Examinations. By PYMNTS | November 18, 2026. |. Banks preparing for exams under the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s new artificial intelligence framework can start by documenting what their AI tools are allowed to do, what customer data they can reach and who can shut them down. In a Tuesday (Nov. 17) analysis , Polsinelli attorney Alexander D. Boyd urged banks to review those controls alongside vendor contracts and incident response plans, particularly where AI agents can change account records or execute transactions. The OCC’s Nov. 4 bulletin gives examiners a framework for evaluating generative and agentic AI, technologies not included in the agencies’ revised model risk management guidance in April. It covers an AI system’s purpose, its risks, and banks’ control, oversight, resilience and assurance. The OCC says the framework creates no new regulatory requirements or supervisory expectations and calls for examiners to tailor their reviews to the materiality of each use case. It applies to national banks, federal savings associations and federal branches and agencies of foreign banks. Polsinelli sees the guide as a way for banks to assess whether their existing controls hold up as AI takes on more authority. Polsinelli recommends cataloging AI already in use and tools under consideration, including features embedded in third-party products. For each use, banks should document the authorized purpose, the data and systems the tool can access, the actions it can take on its own and the decisions that require human approval. The firm also recommends setting approval procedures for new deployments and material changes to existing ones. Banks can then weigh the expected benefits against the potential for customer harm. An AI agent that can move money or access sensitive records may warrant tighter permissions, more extensive testing and human signoff for consequential actions. Polsinelli advises banks to assign clear responsibility for AI activity and monitor systems after deployment. Privacy reviews should trace how a tool accesses, processes and retains customer information and whether it can reproduce or disclose that information in its outputs. Security teams should test whether existing controls can withstand AI-specific threats, including attempts to manipulate an agent through instructions embedded in the content it reads. They should also check whether agents have more access than they need and whether models can expose sensitive data. An existing vendor can add AI features, switch underlying models or introduce agents that interact with bank systems under a contract that predates those capabilities. Polsinelli recommends updating due diligence to identify the models and providers involved, understand how they handle bank and customer data, and review their security controls. Depending on the risk, banks should consider an artificial intelligence addendum that defines permitted uses, limits the use of customer information for model training and addresses downstream providers. The firm also recommends provisions covering notice of material changes and incidents, cooperation with investigations, audit rights and liability for errors or unauthorized actions that harm customers. Polsinelli advises banks to supplement existing incident plans with procedures for identifying, reporting internally, escalating, investigating and remediating AI incidents. An agent could send inaccurate information to customers or execute an unauthorized transaction without triggering conventional alerts for an intrusion or outage. Response procedures should also cover unauthorized AI use, privacy violations, harmful outputs and compromised models. Hong Kong’s banking regulator is exploring AI tools to help compliance teams watch crypto flows for financial crime. The idea is an onchain AI agent that combines crypto monitoring tools with fast fund freezes. No new rule or timeline was announced, and the regulator is taking a cautious first approach to stablecoins. Hong Kong’s banking regulator is weighing whether artificial intelligence (AI) could watch crypto flows for compliance teams, though it has not announced any new rule. Raymond Chan, executive director for enforcement and anti-money laundering (AML) at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) , told a workshop on regulatory technology, or regtech , on Nov. 17 that AML checks could become far more effective if blockchain analytics, customer due-diligence data, scam intelligence, suspicious-wallet monitoring and rapid fund freezes were folded into what he called “an on-chain A. I. agent. ” He posed it as a thought exercise and said the hard part is “linking wallet activities to real-world identities quickly enough to prevent fund dissipation. ”. Chan also said the HKMA is “exploring the development of agentic A. I. ,” meaning software that can carry out multi-step tasks on its own. Such a tool could let banks read onchain transfers next to a customer’s offchain transactions and flag fast back-and-forth swaps between crypto and fiat, a common way to hide a money trail. On stablecoins, Chan said in the same speech that the HKMA is “adopting a cautious initial approach” that puts investor protection and financial-crime controls first. Chan said the same features that make stablecoins useful (a steady price and easy wallet-to-wallet transfers with no intermediary) also draw criminals. Who Is Involved. He pointed to Hong Kong’s Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce (VAIT) , a public-private channel that links the Hong Kong Police, the Customs and Excise Department, the HKMA, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), licensed virtual asset service providers and stablecoin issuers. HKMA Chief Executive Eddie Yue said then that he expected regulated Hong Kong stablecoins to launch in the middle to second half of 2026. Chan also noted that the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global standard setter for AML rules, has made digital assets a key priority as it works to align rules across jurisdictions. title: How P&C insurers can make AI-supported decisions pay off
excerpt: . Giving employees AI tools is the easy part. The returns come from embedding AI into decision-making, building confidence in its outputs, and combining AI with human expertise to improve decisions, with people remaining accountable. Capgemini’s World Property & Casualty Insurance Report 2026 found that nearly half of surveyed property and casualty (P&C) employees said they are comfortable relying on AI recommendations for moderately complex decisions. But comfort is not performance. And 42 percent of insurers track no AI metrics at all, so many cannot say whether those decisions are improving outcomes. Note: Moderately complex decisions include evaluation of standard risks, premium calculation and adjustment, retention or upsell offers, payout or reserve adjustments, product or carrier selection, cross-sell offers. In insurance, the experts (underwriters, claims adjusters, and agents) remain accountable for every decision. The higher the stakes, the more judgment, validation, and oversight they need. If they cannot understand a recommendation, they will not act on it, and adoption stalls. The challenge, then, is not simply to build employees’ confidence in AI, but to embed it in ways that measurably improve decisions and their outcomes. Three shifts can help P&C insurers do that. 1. Redesign workflows to embed AI into decision-making. When AI is used in a standalone app, a chat-style sidebar, or an add-on to the insurance core platforms, experts must go to it manually, switching apps, gathering context, and interpreting outputs before they act. Under tight turnaround times, that demands extra work, and many employees will revert to established workflows instead. The better approach is to redesign the workflow around expert-AI collaboration, with AI operating inside the insurance core platforms where decisions are made. In underwriting, it can combine broker submission data with external risk information, highlight material risk factors, and surface guidance in the underwriter’s workbench. In claims, it can summarize the file, identify missing evidence, and flag cases needing a specialist adjuster. Embedding also allows review checkpoints to be built into the workflow, scaled to the level of risk; routine decisions may only need to be validated, while complex or high-consequence cases should require explicit expert review before proceeding. This allows insurers to scale AI-supported decision-making without treating every underwriting or claims decision as carrying the same level of risk. 2. Design for awareness, not uncertainty. Experts must know how far to rely on what they see. A confident-sounding answer invites overreliance, and an unclear response gets ignored. A Q&A-style sidebar can produce both: fluent answers, without the case context or supporting evidence experts need to judge them. Recommendations embedded in the workflow, alongside that evidence, let experts calibrate how far to rely on them. Good design starts by labeling AI-generated outputs clearly and showing how they were produced by revealing key risk factors, supporting evidence, data sources, and material uncertainty. Not just an answer or a confidence score. Labels should distinguish information from required action. Like road signs that each prompt one clear response – stop, look, and proceed – a clearly labeled AI-generated value or recommendation nudges experts to pause, review, and reconsider before acting. For underwriters and claims adjusters, this distinction matters because an AI recommendation should inform professional judgement, not obscure where accountability for the decision sits. Experts should be encouraged to review, challenge, and refine outputs, and their feedback should shape the design. Artificial intelligence is accelerating development at Summit Financial , but executive vice president Michael D’Amico believes that its lasting value depends on the foundations beneath it. The US wealth management business is investing in engineering and data capabilities to help advisors work more effectively across fragmented systems. Its ambition extends beyond introducing individual tools: Summit wants an integrated information layer that can support changing technologies and better client engagement. Connecting the information For D’Amico, the challenge begins with bringing together information from customer relationship management, portfolio reporting, custody, billing and compensation systems. Differences in how those platforms organise information matter. A household defined one way for billing may be treated differently in reporting or the CRM. Without understanding those distinctions, an AI-generated answer can mislead. Summit’s ambition is what D’Amico calls “central command”: a single location where advisors can obtain insights across client relationships, holdings, strategies and associated billing, he says. That emphasis echoes earlier coverage in this series, including AI’s Value In Wealth Management Starts With Better Processes , in which Bentley Reid’s Kevin Andrews discussed the importance of preparing processes and data for practical adoption. Faster development, measured deployment Summit is already seeing changes in the speed of internal development. D’Amico described rebuilding a complex trade ticket application: engineers initially estimated six to eight weeks, then returned with something to show after one week. The example illustrates shorter development cycles; it does not establish that a finished application was deployed within that period. Summit has also introduced AI capabilities connected to selected systems, including Microsoft tools, CRM and performance reporting. However, D’Amico distinguishes progress internally from adoption across advisor teams. “I would still say we're closer to the beginning,” he said. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has approved 28 charter applications in the past two years, “with several dozen more in the pipeline,” Gould said. Put another way, the agency received as many charter applications in 2025 as it did in the previous four years, the OCC chief noted. “A functional chartering process allows the banking system to renew itself and remain dynamic,” Gould said. “It brings new capital and new ideas into institutions subject to federal supervision. That is especially important as technology changes how Americans expect to receive financial services. ”. 2. AI. Just as banks are not required to distinguish AI as its own risk category, the OCC won’t treat banks’ embrace of AI separately as it relates to evaluating risk, Gould said. Rather, AI is “a component of preexisting business operations and practices,” and the OCC intends to maintain a “right-size approach to innovation,” Gould said. “Supervisory judgment should reflect what new technology does and the potential consequences of its use,” he said. “As that technology evolves, the OCC’s workforce and approach will evolve with it. ”. 3.
